title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: L is a totally ordered set (a 'ligne'), and the page belongs to a 1-dimensional combinatorial set-up for 'réseaux via découpages'. A ps. tr. (pseudo-tronçon / pseudo-transversal) is a convex subset T of L whose boundary ∂T (its endpoints sup/inf, which exist in L) is finite. Page 27 defines T < T' (every t in T is below every t' in T'). With a = Sup T and b = Inf T' one has a ≤ b. T and T' 'se raccordent' (abut) when a = b and exactly one of T, T' contains this point. T ≪ T' means T < T' with a proper gap between them.

Proposition (this page). Take T < T', a = Sup T, b = Inf T'. The following are equivalent:
(a) T and T' do not abut, i.e. (a ∈ T or b ∈ T') ⇒ a ≠ b.
(b) There is x ∈ L with T ⊂ L_{<x} and T' ⊂ L_{>x}. The marginal NB notes that (b) already forces T < T'.
(c) There is a ps. tr. S with T < S < T' such that T abuts S and S abuts T'.
Moreover S is unique, ∂S = {a, b}, and S = {x : T ⊂ L_{<x}, T' ⊂ L_{>x}}, the set of strict separators. S is called the interstitial ps. tr. between T and T'. Concretely, S is the 'gap' interval between a and b: it contains a iff a ∉ T and contains b iff b ∉ T'. For example, if a = b lies in neither set, S = {a}.

Cor 1. If T is strictly bounded below, the set S of strict lower bounds {x : T ⊂ L_{>x}} is a ps. tr. It is characterised by three conditions: S < T, S abuts T, and S has no lower bound. That is, S is the initial ray complementary to T on the left.

Cor 2. S is called the left interstitial ps. tr. of T; the right one is defined dually when T is bounded above.

Purpose: these gap intervals let one fill in the complement of a finite disjoint family of intervals. Page 29 uses them to show that finite ≪-disjoint families of tranches are determined by their unions ('modules'), with a relative frontier and a set of 'components' π0.
errors: Implicit density hypothesis. Take a ∈ T and b ∈ T' with a < b and nothing strictly between them in L (L discrete). Then (a) holds, since a ≠ b, but (b) fails and no nonempty interstitial S exists. So the equivalence needs L dense, or S = ∅ must be allowed, or 'raccordement' must be redefined to cover successor pairs. Presumably L is a dense line (ℝ-like or real-closed) in the intended setting, but this is not stated on the page.
Cor 1 tacitly assumes T is nonempty and that the infimum of T exists in L, so that the strict-minorant set has a boundary point. This is consistent with the definition of ps. tr. but not stated.

ideas.what: Gap (interstitial) interval between two separated convex subsets of a totally ordered set, characterised by abutting on both sides
ideas.modern_name: complementary intervals / gaps in a linear order; cell decomposition of a line (o-minimal 1-dim cell decomposition)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore order theory; in tame-topology form van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight (1980s)
ideas.where_published: Not published; the tame-topology programme is only sketched in Esquisse d'un programme (1984)

ideas.what: Left/right interstitial ray of a bounded interval (set of strict minorants or majorants)

deep.surprise_reason: Elementary order-theoretic bookkeeping (gaps between intervals on a line) in preparation for a combinatorial decomposition formalism. It is correct up to an unstated density assumption and has no novel content beyond its place in Grothendieck's unpublished 1986 'réseaux' set-up.
